title: CEC forecasting, benchmarking and generation review
scope: California electricity planning, covered buildings and onsite thermal generation.
whatItDoes: IEPR forecasts incorporate utility data-center applications. Covered buildings over 50,000 square feet report annual energy use. Thermal generation of 50 MW or more falls within CEC licensing jurisdiction.
environmentalApplication: Connect load forecasts with procurement, local permitting and backup-generator impacts.
limitation: CEC does not permit data centers themselves. A small-power-plant exemption still requires environmental review and subsequent permits.
researchQuestion: How do projected connections compare with realized demand and local pollution?

title: AB 1577: facility energy reporting
scope: Data centers ≥10 MW; specified public, research and utility facilities excluded.
whatItDoes: Requires energy, peak-load, PUE and fuel reporting; CEC sets filing timing. Public releases are anonymized aggregates; IEPR load-trend assessments start in 2029.
environmentalApplication: Local discretionary applications must estimate electricity, onsite generation and boundary noise.
limitation: Facility reporting does not isolate AI workloads; customer energy data remain protected.
researchQuestion: Can aggregate disclosures reveal infrastructure pressure while retaining useful local accountability?

title: AB 2469: water conditions for development
scope: Construction or expansion increasing maximum peak water use; discretionary and ministerial approvals.
whatItDoes: Requires water-supply assessment, projected use, efficiency and workforce disclosures, and applicant funding of necessary water infrastructure. Water-scarcity plans begin January 1, 2028.
environmentalApplication: Evaluate dry-year reliability alongside project demand and infrastructure costs.
limitation: No MW cutoff appears here; satisfying conditions does not require approval.
researchQuestion: Are peak cooling demands compatible with enforceable drought reductions and existing customers' needs?

title: AB 2619: water-use disclosure
authority: Cities, counties and water suppliers; chapter 437
scope: Data centers across defined size classes, including facilities below 2 MW.
whatItDoes: Initial licensing requires good-faith water estimates and source disclosure; renewals report prior-year water use, direct use by source and cooling type.
environmentalApplication: Supplier shortage planning must include unconstrained demand from data centers and other large users.
limitation: Withdrawals or deliveries are not automatically consumptive losses or upstream electricity water use.
researchQuestion: How accurately do license estimates predict metered seasonal demand?

title: SB 886: interconnection and cost protection
scope: Participating data-center customers; transmission-specific provisions cover new agreements from January 1, 2027.
whatItDoes: Requires tariffs or updated rules by January 1, 2028 to prevent stranded costs and cost shifts. Transmission provisions allocate upgrade costs, constrain refunds and require termination protection.
environmentalApplication: Compare committed demand, infrastructure exposure and demand-response participation.
limitation: Implementation requires CPUC decisions; transmission cost allocation is constrained by federal law.
researchQuestion: Do deposits and exit obligations cover realistic cancellation and underutilization scenarios?

title: AB 2383: service tariffs and procurement
authority: CPUC, CCAs and energy service providers; chapter 435
scope: Participating customers; generation-tariff thresholds must be set no higher than 25 MW.
whatItDoes: Requires cost-protective service tariffs, clean-energy-consistent procurement and generation payment mechanisms lasting at least ten years. CCA/provider generation tariffs are due January 1, 2028.
environmentalApplication: Link added load with incremental procurement, collateral and societal-cost contributions.
limitation: Generation-specific exemptions and thresholds are not universal exemptions from every provision.
researchQuestion: Which contract terms best prevent stranded procurement without weakening clean-energy requirements?

title: SB 1168: rate-structure assessment
scope: Data-center transmission and distribution connections in CPUC proceedings.
whatItDoes: Requires assessing opportunities for rates that assign reasonable network costs and proportionate load-growth procurement costs to data centers while relieving residential rate pressures.
environmentalApplication: Connect resource planning to distributional effects on households, including CARE and FERA participants.
limitation: The act directs assessment; it neither publishes a completed tariff nor establishes a numerical cost allocation.
researchQuestion: How do allocation choices affect low-income customers under different load-growth outcomes?

title: SB 887: CEQA review and conditional streamlining
authority: Lead agencies, Governor and LCI; chapter 439
scope: Data-center entitlements; categorical-exemption restrictions contain specified facility exceptions.
whatItDoes: Extends CEQA coverage and bars categorical exemptions for covered projects. Leadership-project streamlining requires demanding energy, water, cost-protection and community-benefit conditions.
environmentalApplication: Streamlining conditions include hourly zero-carbon supply within five years, predominantly new resources, and efficient cooling.
limitation: These streamlining conditions are not universal operating standards for every data center.
researchQuestion: Do enforceable project conditions reduce cumulative burdens beyond statutory minimum review?

title: SB 57: earlier cost-shift assessment
scope: Electrical-corporation costs caused by new data-center loads.
whatItDoes: Authorizes assessment of procurement, network investment and stranded-asset cost shifts. Any completed assessment must be submitted to legislative committees and posted by January 1, 2027.
environmentalApplication: Provides an analytical bridge between electricity growth, infrastructure risk and ratepayer protection.
limitation: SB 57 authorizes assessment; it does not itself order a new tariff. Section sunsets January 1, 2031.
researchQuestion: Which documented cost risks warrant specific safeguards in later tariff proceedings?

title: AB 93: vetoed water proposal
whatItDoes: The Governor returned AB 93 without approval. It must not be displayed as an operative water-reporting mandate.
environmentalApplication: Compare the unsuccessful 2025 proposal with the separately enacted 2026 water-disclosure laws, AB 2469 and AB 2619.
limitation: A vetoed proposal supplies legislative context, not compliance authority; later bills require independent scope and effective-date checks.
researchQuestion: What changed between the vetoed proposal and the enacted water protections?

title: CalEnviroScreen 5.0: cumulative-burden screening
status: Final tool; not a facility permit
scope: California census-tract pollution burden and population vulnerability.
whatItDoes: Updates screening data and methods, adding diabetes prevalence and small air-toxic sites. It informs CalEPA's final September 18, 2026 disadvantaged-community designation.
environmentalApplication: Screen proposed sites, then investigate nearby receptors, emissions, noise and community priorities.
limitation: A screening percentile neither measures a project's incremental health risk nor determines permit approval.
researchQuestion: Would the project add burdens where exposure and vulnerability already overlap?

title: DWR: supplier shortage and drought planning
scope: Urban suppliers exceeding 3,000 connections or 3,000 acre-feet annually.
whatItDoes: Requires annual supply-demand assessment and shortage reporting, generally by July 1; specified imported-water allocation timing can extend submission.
environmentalApplication: Use supplier assessments, shortage-contingency plans and drought-risk assessments to contextualize new cooling demand.
limitation: Regional or statewide sufficiency does not establish site-specific supply. Assessments require ongoing updates as actual conditions change.
researchQuestion: What restrictions apply when facility demand peaks during a supplier shortage?

title: SB 253: corporate emissions disclosure
status: Enacted statute; subsequent regulatory approval unverified
scope: U.S. entities doing business in California with annual revenue above $1 billion.
whatItDoes: Requires Scope 1–2 reporting in 2026 and Scope 3 from 2027. CARB's September notice identifies November 10, 2026, conditional on OAL approval.
environmentalApplication: Use corporate emissions to supplement facility and supply-chain evidence.
limitation: Corporate totals are not facility or AI-model measurements. This review did not establish whether OAL approved the regulation after CARB’s September 1 notice.
researchQuestion: Can corporate inventories be reconciled with location-specific electricity and equipment emissions?
